entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11677"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 34</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.34.1-Ezek.34.31">Eze 34:1-31</reference>. Reproof of the False Shepherds; Promise of the True and Good Shepherd.</title> <div sID="gen21153" type="x-p"/> Having in the thirty-third chapter laid down repentance as the necessary preliminary to happier times for the people, He now promises the removal of the false shepherds as preparatory to the raising up of the Good Shepherd.<div eID="gen21153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11677"/>2. <reference osisRef="Jer.23.1">Jr 23:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Zech.11.17">Zec 11:17</reference> similarly make the removal of the false shepherds the preliminary to the interposition of Messiah the Good Shepherd in behalf of His people Israel. The "shepherds" are not prophets or priests, but rulers who sought in their government their own selfish ends, not the good of the people ruled. The term was appropriate, as David, the first king and the type of the true David (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">24</reference>), was taken from being a shepherd (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.2">2Sa 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.70">Psa 78:70</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.71">71</reference>); and the office, like that of a shepherd for his flock, is to guard and provide for his people. The choice of a shepherd for the first king was therefore designed to suggest this thought, just as Jesus' selection of fishermen for apostles was designed to remind them of their spiritual office of catching men (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Is 44:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.8">Jr 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.15">3:15</reference>; 10:21; 23:1, 2). <div eID="gen21154" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 34 Eze 34:1-31 . Reproof of the False Shepherds; Promise of the True and Good Shepherd. Having in the thirty-third chapter laid down repentance as the necessary preliminary to happier times for the people, He now promises the removal of the false shepherds as preparatory to the raising up of the Good Shepherd. 2. Jr 23:1 and Zec 11:17 similarly make the removal of the false shepherds the preliminary to the interposition of Messiah the Good Shepherd in behalf of His people Israel. The "shepherds" are not prophets or priests, but rulers who sought in their government their own selfish ends, not the good of the people ruled. The term was appropriate, as David, the first king and the type of the true David ( Eze 34:23 , 24 ), was taken from being a shepherd ( 2Sa 5:2 ; Psa 78:70 , 71 ); and the office, like that of a shepherd for his flock, is to guard and provide for his people. The choice of a shepherd for the first king was therefore designed to suggest this thought, just as Jesus' selection of fishermen for apostles was designed to remind them of their spiritual office of catching men (compare Is 44:28 ; Jr 2:8 ; 3:15 ; 10:21; 23:1, 2).

He then defines the class about to be punitively "judged," namely, "the rams and he-goats," or "great he-goats" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Is 14:9</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.3">Zec 10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.32">Mt 25:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.33">33</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11697"/><div sID="gen21191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11697"/><hi type="bold">26. them and the places round about my hill--</hi>The Jews, and Zion, God's hill (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>), are to be sources of blessing, not merely to themselves, but to the surrounding heathen (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.24">Is 19:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.56.6">56:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.3">60:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.13">Zec 8:13</reference>). The literal fulfilment is, however, the primary one, though the spiritual also is designed. In correspondence with the settled reign of righteousness internally, all is to be prosperity externally, fertilizing showers (according to the promise of the ancient covenant, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.4">Le 26:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.9">Psa 68:9</reference>; Mal 3:10), and productive trees and lands (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.27">Eze 34:27</reference>). Thus shall they realize the image of <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.14">Eze 34:14</reference>; namely, a flock richly pastured by God Himself. <div eID="gen21191" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11700"/><div sID="gen21194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11700"/><hi type="bold">29. plant of renown--</hi>Messiah, the "Rod" and "Branch" (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Is 11:1</reference>), the "righteous Branch" (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>), who shall obtain for them "renown." Fairbairn less probably translates, "A plantation for a name," that is, a flourishing condition, represented as a garden (alluding to Eden, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.8-Gen.2.11">Ge 2:8-11</reference>, with its various trees, good for food and pleasant to the sight), the planting of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">Is 60:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">61:3</reference>), and an object of "renown" among the heathen. <div eID="gen21194" type="x-p"/>

But as God had promised many things which mere "men" could not expect to realize, He shows that it is not from man's might their realization is to be looked for, but from God, who would perform them for His covenant-people, "His flock" [Rosenmuller]. When we realize most our weakness and God's power and faithfulness to His covenant, we are in the fittest state for receiving His blessings. <chapter eID="Ezek.34"/>
